Anterior nuclei of thalamus.definition: A group of thalamic nuclei that forms an important relay within limbic memory circuitry.
functions: Relays hippocampal and mammillary-body related signals toward cingulate cortex.
Contributes to episodic memory and contextual processing.
clinical: Damage can contribute to anterograde and contextual memory impairment.
Part of the Papez circuit; circuit-level models should not be interpreted as a single-region explanation for psychiatric disorders.
Anterior nuclei of thalamus.exam: Anterior thalamic nuclei → mammillothalamic/cingulate limbic circuitry → memory.

Anterior cingulate cortex.definition: Medial frontal cortical region involved in cognitive control, motivation, affective processing and autonomic integration.
functions: Monitors conflict, errors and salient internal or external events.
Supports motivation, effort allocation and affective/autonomic responses.
clinical: Dysfunction is implicated across several psychiatric disorders, but findings are network-level and not diagnostically specific.
Important in models of depression, OCD, addiction and schizophrenia involving salience, control and motivation.
Anterior cingulate cortex.exam: Think monitoring, motivation, conflict/error processing and affective control.

Amygdala.definition: A group of medial temporal nuclei that assigns emotional and motivational significance to sensory information.
functions: Supports threat detection and fear learning.
Contributes to emotional memory and modulation of autonomic/endocrine responses.
clinical: Central to fear/anxiety circuitry and emotional learning.
Altered amygdala activity is reported in multiple disorders but is neither necessary nor sufficient for diagnosis.
Amygdala.exam: Amygdala = emotional salience, threat/fear learning and emotional memory.

Hippocampus.definition: A medial temporal allocortical structure essential for forming and retrieving contextual and episodic memories.
functions: Encodes and retrieves contextual relationships within episodic memory.
Interacts with cortical networks during memory consolidation and retrieval.
clinical: Bilateral hippocampal injury causes prominent anterograde episodic-memory impairment.
Stress, depression, epilepsy and neurodegenerative disease can involve hippocampal structural or functional changes, with disorder-specific evidence varying.
Hippocampus.exam: Hippocampus → episodic/contextual memory; fornix is a major output pathway.

Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.definition: Lateral prefrontal association cortex supporting executive control and goal-directed cognition.
functions: Working memory and manipulation of information.
Planning, cognitive flexibility, inhibition of competing responses and goal maintenance.
clinical: Executive-control dysfunction is described across schizophrenia, ADHD, depression and other conditions.
Psychiatric symptoms should be interpreted as network phenomena rather than lesions of a single named area.
Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.exam: DLPFC → working memory, planning, set shifting and executive control.

Orbitofrontal cortex.definition: Ventromedial prefrontal association cortex that evaluates reward, punishment and changing outcome value.
functions: Updates the expected value of outcomes.
Supports flexible decision-making when reward contingencies change.
clinical: Orbitofrontal dysfunction is relevant to disinhibition and maladaptive reward-based decision-making.
It is also studied in OCD and addiction within broader cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical networks.
Orbitofrontal cortex.exam: OFC → outcome value, reversal learning, reward/punishment-guided behaviour.

Insula.definition: A buried cortical region involved in interoception, salience, taste and integration of bodily and emotional signals.
functions: Represents internal bodily states and contributes to conscious interoception.
Integrates salient sensory, autonomic and affective information.
clinical: The insula is a major node of salience and interoceptive networks.
Relevant to anxiety, panic, addiction, pain and awareness of bodily states.
Insula.exam: Insula → interoception + salience + integration of bodily/affective signals.

Nucleus accumbens.definition: A ventral striatal region integrating limbic information with motivational and action-selection systems.
functions: Contributes to reward learning, incentive motivation and reinforcement.
Integrates cortical, limbic and dopaminergic signals.
clinical: Important in contemporary models of addiction and reward-related behaviour.
Dopamine signalling here is better understood as contributing to salience, prediction and reinforcement than as a simple 'pleasure centre'.
Nucleus accumbens.exam: VTA dopamine → nucleus accumbens is a key mesolimbic reward/motivation pathway.

Caudate nucleus.definition: A component of the dorsal striatum involved in action selection, associative learning and cognitive control.
functions: Integrates cortical information into basal-ganglia action-selection loops.
Contributes to habit learning, goal-directed behaviour and cognitive flexibility.
clinical: Cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops involving the caudate are relevant to OCD and other disorders of repetitive behaviour and cognitive control.
Striatal dysfunction also contributes to movement and neurodegenerative disorders.
Caudate nucleus.exam: Caudate → associative/cognitive striatum; putamen is more strongly linked to sensorimotor loops.

Putamen.definition: A major component of the dorsal striatum with prominent sensorimotor and associative connections.
functions: Helps select and scale motor programmes.
Participates in habit learning and corticostriatal reinforcement loops.
clinical: Degeneration or dysfunction of striatal circuits produces characteristic motor and behavioural changes.
Striatal circuitry is also relevant to tic disorders, OCD and addiction.

Globus pallidus.definition: A major basal-ganglia output/relay structure regulating thalamocortical activity.
functions: The internal pallidal segment provides inhibitory output toward thalamic and brainstem targets.
Helps regulate selection and suppression of competing motor programmes.
clinical: Basal-ganglia circuit dysfunction can produce hypokinetic or hyperkinetic movement disorders.
The internal segment is an established deep-brain-stimulation target in selected movement disorders.
Globus pallidus.exam: GPi is a major inhibitory output node of the basal ganglia.

Thalamus.definition: A paired diencephalic structure containing multiple nuclei that relay and transform information between subcortical systems and cortex.
functions: Relays sensory, motor, limbic and cognitive information through nucleus-specific circuits.
Contributes to attention, arousal and cortical state regulation.
clinical: Thalamic lesions can produce sensory, cognitive, arousal and movement syndromes depending on the nucleus affected.
Thalamocortical dysregulation is a recurring concept in models of schizophrenia, sleep and consciousness.
Thalamus.exam: Do not treat the thalamus as one functional unit: thalamic nuclei have distinct connectivity and roles.

Hypothalamus.definition: A small diencephalic region that integrates autonomic, endocrine, homeostatic and behavioural signals.
functions: Regulates temperature, hunger, thirst, circadian timing and reproductive/endocrine functions.
Controls pituitary function and coordinates autonomic responses.
clinical: Hypothalamic dysfunction can disturb sleep, appetite, endocrine function and thermoregulation.
It links emotional states with autonomic and endocrine responses.

Ventral tegmental area.definition: A midbrain dopaminergic region that provides major projections to limbic and prefrontal targets.
functions: Supports reinforcement learning, motivation, salience and adaptive behavioural responses.
Provides dopaminergic input to mesolimbic and mesocortical circuits.
clinical: Dopaminergic VTA projections are central to reward and reinforcement models.
Dopamine pathways involving the midbrain are also relevant to psychosis and antipsychotic pharmacology.
Ventral tegmental area.exam: VTA → mesolimbic/mesocortical dopamine; distinguish pathway from receptor-specific effects.

Substantia nigra.definition: A midbrain structure containing dopaminergic neurons and other neuronal populations; pars compacta provides major nigrostriatal dopamine.
functions: Nigrostriatal dopamine modulates basal-ganglia motor and action-selection circuits.
Other substantia-nigra components participate in basal-ganglia output and motor control.
clinical: Loss of substantia-nigra pars compacta dopaminergic neurons is a core pathology of Parkinson disease.
Nigrostriatal dopamine blockade contributes to extrapyramidal adverse effects of antipsychotics.
Substantia nigra.exam: Nigrostriatal dopamine: substantia nigra pars compacta → striatum.

Raphe nuclei.definition: A distributed group of brainstem nuclei containing the brain's major serotonergic cell populations.
functions: Modulate mood, arousal, sleep-wake regulation, pain and behavioural flexibility.
Provide widespread serotonergic projections throughout the brain and spinal cord.
clinical: Serotonergic systems are targets of SSRIs, SNRIs and several other psychotropics.
Serotonin should not be reduced to a single 'mood chemical'; receptor subtype, circuit and treatment context matter.
Raphe nuclei.exam: Raphe nuclei → major source of central serotonin.

Locus coeruleus.definition: A pontine nucleus containing the brain's principal noradrenergic neurons.
functions: Modulates arousal, attention, vigilance and stress-related responses.
Provides widespread noradrenergic projections to cortex, hippocampus, cerebellum and spinal cord.
clinical: Noradrenergic systems are involved in attention, arousal and stress responses.
Relevant to pharmacology of antidepressants, ADHD medications and drugs affecting autonomic arousal.
Locus coeruleus.exam: Locus coeruleus → principal brainstem source of noradrenaline.

Corpus callosum.definition: The largest commissural white-matter tract connecting homologous and related cortical regions across the cerebral hemispheres.
functions: Enables interhemispheric transfer and integration of cortical information.
Supports coordinated bilateral sensorimotor and cognitive processing.
clinical: Callosal lesions can produce disconnection syndromes depending on location.
Callosal anatomy is an important reference point when interpreting structural neuroimaging.
Corpus callosum.exam: Corpus callosum = largest commissural pathway between cerebral hemispheres.

Arcuate fasciculus.definition: A long association-fibre system linking frontal and temporal language-related cortical regions within a hemisphere.
functions: Supports communication between posterior temporal and frontal language networks.
Participates in speech-language processing and repetition through a broader distributed network.
clinical: Classically associated with conduction aphasia when the relevant language network is disrupted.
Modern language neuroscience treats language as a distributed network rather than a single tract-to-symptom mapping.
Arcuate fasciculus.exam: Arcuate fasciculus is a major intrahemispheric language association pathway.

Fornix.definition: A major white-matter output pathway of the hippocampal formation.
functions: Carries hippocampal formation signals toward mammillary bodies and septal/basal forebrain regions.
Forms an important connection within memory circuitry.
clinical: Fornix injury can impair memory through disruption of hippocampal output.
It is a useful tract to recognize when studying the Papez circuit.
Fornix.exam: Hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies is a classic memory-circuit relationship.

Cerebellum.definition: A hindbrain structure that compares intended and ongoing actions to refine motor, cognitive and affective processes.
functions: Coordinates movement, timing, balance and motor learning.
Cerebellar connections also support language, cognition and affect.
clinical: Cerebellar lesions can cause ataxia, dysmetria, dysarthria and nystagmus.
Cerebellar contributions to cognition and psychiatric symptoms are an active area of research and should be described as network contributions.
Cerebellum.exam: Cerebellum is not purely motor: posterior cerebellar networks participate in cognition and affect.
